procedures.title: Heated grips not working
procedures.summary: Step-by-step electrical check of a motorcycle's heated grips: fuse, switch, supply voltage and heating element.
procedures.source: General automotive electrical practice written for OpenDiag. Values marked 'general guidance' are not manufacturer specifications.

steps.text: Are the heated grips factory-fitted (controlled from the dashboard or a handlebar switch supplied with the bike)?
steps.help: Aftermarket grips have their own controller; check its instructions too.

steps.text: Aftermarket grips are powered through their own controller. Continue with the same checks, using the controller's instructions for its fuse and connectors.
Do any warning lights show on the dashboard, or did the scan find fault codes?
steps.help: Many bikes switch off accessories when the battery voltage is low. Run Scan Vehicle first if you have not.

steps.text: Look at the fault codes first. A low system voltage code (such as P0562) explains grips that switch off: many bikes disable heated grips to protect the battery.
Measure the battery voltage with the engine running at a fast idle (about 3000 rpm).
steps.help: Multimeter on DC volts, red probe on +, black on −.

spec.source: Typical 12 V charging system range (general guidance; check your bike's manual)

steps.text: Find the heated grip fuse (see the fuse box lid or manual). Is it intact?
Unplug one grip's connector. With the ignition on and the grips switched to high, measure the voltage on the supply side of the connector.
steps.help: Use back-probe pins; do not force the probe into the connector.

measurement.source: Should be close to the battery voltage you measured (within about 1 V; general guidance)

steps.text: Measure the resistance of the grip's heating element across its two connector pins (connector unplugged, ignition off). Enter the specification from your service manual when asked.

measurement.source: Specification entered from your service manual

charging-low.text: The charging voltage is below the typical range. A weak battery or charging fault can make the bike switch off the heated grips. Have the battery and charging system checked first.

charging-high.text: The charging voltage is above the typical range, which points to a regulator fault. This can damage electronics: have it checked before continuing.

fuse.text: The fuse has blown. Replace it with one of the same rating. If it blows again there is a short circuit in the grips or wiring: do not fit a bigger fuse.

supply.text: Power is not reaching the grip. Likely places: the grip switch or controller, its relay, or the wiring and connectors between them.

controller.text: Power arrives and the element's resistance is within your specification, so the element is probably fine. Check the connector for corrosion and the controller/switch output under load.

element-short.text: The element's resistance is below the specification: it is probably shorted. The grip (element) likely needs replacing.

element-open.text: The element's resistance is above the specification or open: the element or its wiring inside the grip is probably broken.

procedures.title: Battery and charging check
procedures.summary: Check a 12 V battery and the charging system with a multimeter, and compare with the voltage the vehicle reports.
procedures.source: General 12 V lead-acid battery practice written for OpenDiag (general guidance, not manufacturer specifications). Lithium batteries and start-stop systems may differ.

steps.text: With the engine off for at least an hour, measure the battery voltage.

spec.source: A charged 12 V lead-acid battery usually rests at about 12.4–12.9 V (general guidance)

steps.text: The battery is low or discharged. Charge it fully and measure again before judging the battery. Continue to check the charging system.
Start the engine and measure the battery voltage at a fast idle. You can also read the vehicle's 'Control module voltage' in Live Data.

spec.source: Typical charging range (general guidance; some smart-charging systems run lower)

ok.text: Battery and charging voltages are within the general ranges. If problems continue, a load test of the battery is the next step.

charge-low.text: The charging voltage is low. Possible causes: alternator/regulator fault, slipping drive belt, poor connections. Some vehicles with smart charging deliberately run lower, so check the vehicle's specification.

charge-high.text: The charging voltage is high, pointing to a regulator fault. Have it checked soon: overvoltage can damage electronics.

procedures.title: Engine running lean (P0171 / P0174)
procedures.summary: Use live fuel trims to tell an air leak from a fuel delivery problem.
procedures.source: General fuel trim diagnosis practice written for OpenDiag (general guidance).

steps.text: Is the engine at normal operating temperature (coolant about 80–100 °C)?
Let the engine warm up first: fuel trims are only meaningful in closed loop.
At idle, read short term + long term fuel trim for bank 1 and add them together. Enter the total.

spec.source: Total trim within about ±10 % is usually considered normal (general guidance)

steps.text: Hold the engine at about 2500 rpm and enter the total fuel trim again.

measurement.source: Compared with the idle value: a total that drops by more than about 5 points at higher speed suggests extra air at idle (general guidance)

vacuum.text: Trims improve at higher engine speed. That points to unmetered air at idle: check vacuum hoses, intake gaskets, the crankcase breather and the brake booster hose.

fuel.text: Trims stay high at higher engine speed. That points to fuel delivery or air flow measurement: check fuel pressure, injectors and the air flow sensor.
